questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Patronage and the subject of a picture
questions.learningObjective: Identify which patronage factor explains the subject a patron chose
questions.stem: In a structural brief for a civic hall canopy, the client asks why the soffit panel shows the town founders instead of the guild trades.

options.text: The subject was chosen so the canopy would state the patron's civic ideals to everyone entering.
The subject was bound by an old guild rule, so every canopy in the city repeats the same design.
options.misconception: assumes the subject was fixed by rule and could not be changed

options.text: The subject was chosen because that square of the ceiling was the cheapest one left to decorate.
options.misconception: explains the subject by cost rather than by intended meaning

options.text: The subject was copied directly from a panel already in the town's archive store.
options.misconception: assumes the design was a straight copy of an older panel

questions.explanation: The patron sets the brief, so the subject serves the patron's message. The guild-rule and cheapest-panel readings ignore that each patron renegotiated the subject for the new building.
questions.hint: Ask who paid for the canopy and what they wanted it to say.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission and its stated purpose
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what a list of stated purposes establishes about separate commissions
questions.stem: A commission log for six new civic ceilings records a stated purpose for each: public virtue, commemoration, decoration, instruction, veneration and civic pride.

options.text: Each commission named the use its image was meant to serve, so purpose varies with the patron's brief.
The word decoration appears most often, so the images were made mainly to look attractive.
options.misconception: reads one listed purpose as the dominant motive of all six

options.text: Six different purposes were recorded, so the images carry no relationship to the brief at all.
options.misconception: treats varied stated purposes as evidence of no brief at all

options.text: Veneration and civic pride are opposites, so the log must have been written carelessly.
options.misconception: treats two listed purposes as mutually exclusive errors

questions.explanation: Each entry ties an image to a particular use and audience. Treating one entry as the motive of all six mistakes a list of briefs for a single verdict.
questions.hint: Read each line as a separate brief, not a shared aim.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a window is made legible to a non-reading congregation
questions.stem: A parish architect is planning a nave of stained glass and wants to know why a mediaeval congregation could read such a window as a story.

answer.exemplar: Congregations read these windows as sequential narrative because the tiers of figures, the order of scenes, and the placement of saints and donors all guide the eye through a coherent cycle from one episode to the next, so the window functioned as a visual text.

questions.explanation: The window was built as a sequence a viewer could follow, not a decorative panel. Reading such a work as a single image misses how the tiers of figures organise the narrative.
questions.hint: Think about how the eye is guided between successive scenes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the legible length of an inscription from measured losses
questions.stem: A survey of a dedicatory inscription records 12.0 m of lettering with 0.6 m lost at each end, and the letter unit repeats every 0.6 m; how many complete units remain?
questions.explanation: Readable length is 12.0 minus 0.6 at each end, which is 10.8 m, and 10.8 divided by the 0.6 m unit gives 18. Counting the whole 12.0 m would include the worn ends.
questions.hint: Subtract the lost ends before dividing by the unit.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A court image and its political claim
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the political claim carried by a ranked court programme

stimulus.body: A court's engraved programme lists the ruler seated above eleven dignitaries in strict order of rank. The ruler is given a larger scale and a raised tier, while the other figures share one level. The survey notes 5.2 m of wall reserved for the ruler alone on a panel 20 m long.

questions.stem: Given this programme, what political claim does the court image make?

options.text: The ruler outranks everyone present, and the image is built to make that hierarchy visible at a glance.
The ruler's larger scale shows that the artist worked in a more advanced technique than his colleagues.
options.misconception: reads scale as a sign of technique rather than of rank

options.text: The eleven dignitaries were added to the panel later, which proves the composition was not planned.
options.misconception: infers unplanned composition from figures in the scheme

options.text: The raised tier shows the panel was painted for a stairwell, since tiers imply architecture.
options.misconception: links a visual device to building fabric without evidence

questions.explanation: Scale, tier and ordered placement together assert rank. The technique, careless-planning and stairwell readings each take one formal device and detach it from the hierarchy.
questions.hint: Ask what the ruler's size and elevation do together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether dated working habits can place a panel in time
questions.stem: First decide which features of a painting show the period it was made in; then, for a facade panel dated by its tooling marks, choose the reading that holds.

options.text: Regular tool marks and stock proportions sit close to the body of work of the workshop's own decade.
The panel imitates an older court type so exactly that its date must belong to the older century.
options.misconception: concludes an earlier date from the choice of an old model

options.text: Tool marks record only the tools available, so they carry no information about when a panel was made.
options.misconception: denies that working methods can date a work at all

options.text: Stock proportions show the panel was made for export, so the local date must be the buyer's date.
options.misconception: reads a market for the work as a date for its making

questions.explanation: Period style is read from method as well as motif, and a panel's working habits place it in time. The imitation, tools-only and export readings each mistake a choice for a date.
questions.hint: Separate what records making from what records taste.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a deliberate revival of an older style accomplishes
questions.stem: A facade engineer is told that a new civic hall borrows the column order of an earlier building; what best describes such a deliberate revival?

options.text: An older visual language is adopted on purpose to link the new building to a valued precedent.
The older forms are copied because the builders had no training in any later style.
options.misconception: assumes the revival is a symptom of ignorance

options.text: The older forms are a temporary measure that the site owner plans to remove in a later phase.
options.misconception: treats a deliberate style as a provisional placeholder

options.text: The older forms prove the earlier building was still standing when the new hall was designed.
options.misconception: infers a physical link that the record does not require

questions.explanation: A revival is a choice to summon an admired precedent. The ignorance, provisional and physical-link readings each substitute a story about cause for the function the style performs.
questions.hint: Ask what the borrowed style achieves for the new building.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the pairing of payer and subject in a survey of doorways
questions.stem: A survey of 24 doorways in a merchant quarter records, at each, who paid for the carving and what the carving shows; what does this paired record establish?

options.text: Subject and payer move together, so the image usually serves the interests of the person who commissioned it.
Subjects change every year with fashion, while payers remain fixed for centuries in the same quarter.
options.misconception: separates subject from payer and blames fashion for content

options.text: Most doorways show religious scenes, so the quarter's owners were a single religious community.
options.misconception: reads one dominant subject as proof of a single owner type

options.text: Payers change with every doorway, so the record shows no link between money and subject at all.
options.misconception: claims a survey showing regular links proves there are none

questions.explanation: Reading payer and subject together shows that content tracks the interest of the commissioner. The fashion, single-community and no-link readings each contradict the regularity recorded.
questions.hint: Look at what happens to the subject when the payer changes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission and its stated purpose
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a stated purpose contributes to a commission record
questions.stem: A client for a new assembly hall wants a brief explaining what a stated purpose achieves for the commission and for the audience.

answer.exemplar: A stated purpose ties the commission to a concrete use: it tells the workshop what to depict, tells the donor what benefit their money buys, and tells the audience how to read the result, so the image does work rather than merely filling a space.

questions.explanation: Purpose sets the content, the fee and the expected reading at once. Treating it as a decorative formula or a private joke strips the commission of the practical agreement.
questions.hint: Think about what the purpose tells the workshop to do.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many narrative units fit a given vault length
questions.stem: In a chapel vault 12.9 m long, the scheme allows 1.5 m per painted roundel and reserves 0.45 m of plain plaster at each end; how many roundels fit?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a later cutting made over an earlier inscription

stimulus.body: A surveyor records a painted inscription on a tomb chest: the name of the dead man, then a line naming his wife, then a date and a phrase asking the living to pray. A second line, cut later into the stone beneath the first, gives a different name. The tomb stands in a church the man's family paid to rebuild in the same decade.

questions.stem: Given this record, what does the cut second line most plainly show?

options.text: Ownership of the monument was contested at some point after the first inscription was set.
The family paid for the church and the tomb, so the second name must belong to the builder.
options.misconception: assumes the second name belongs to whoever paid for the church

options.text: The stone was reused from an older tomb, because names were never carved in two layers.
options.misconception: insists on a single carving episode where two are recorded

options.text: The inscription was written by a clerk who copied the first line without noticing the second.
options.misconception: explains a deliberate change as a clerical error

questions.explanation: A later cutting over an earlier inscription marks a change of claim or ownership. The builder, single-episode and clerical-error readings each ignore the physical order recorded.
questions.hint: Consider what a later cut over an earlier line means.

options.text: Hierarchy of scale, elevation and placement makes the claim visible without needing a caption to explain it.
The paint is unusually rich, so the viewer must read the court as prosperous and therefore rightful.
options.misconception: treats costly materials as the argument the image makes

options.misconception: reads costume as a claim of legitimacy to rule

options.text: The picture hangs in the main hall, so its position proves the intention behind the commission.
options.misconception: treats the hanging place as evidence of intent

questions.explanation: A court image argues through ordered devices that work on a viewer at a glance. The richness, costume and hanging-place readings each mistake a detail for the argument made.
questions.hint: Rank the devices by how directly they carry the claim.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State what a period style is able to record about a work
questions.stem: An engineer surveying a painted ceiling asks what a period style is most useful for recording about the moment of a work.

options.text: The working habits, materials and expectations of the time in which the work was produced.
The personal tastes of the painter, which remain constant throughout a long career.
options.misconception: treats a shared period style as one painter's fixed taste

options.text: The market price the work fetched when it was new, which is recorded in the painting itself.
options.misconception: believes the painting carries its own sale price

options.text: The name later critics gave the period, which every contemporary artist already used.
options.misconception: confuses later period names with names in contemporary use

questions.explanation: A period style records shared working conditions: the materials available, the habits of the shop, the expectations of patrons. The fixed-taste, price and naming readings import what lies outside the work.
questions.hint: Think about what is shared across many makers at one date.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a survey showing when revivals cluster in time
questions.stem: A survey of 40 new facades records for each the date, whether it revived an older style, and the building it revived; what does the survey show?

options.text: Revivals cluster in certain decades, so revival follows periods when older models were newly valued.
Every facade in the survey revives an older style, proving that the style was never abandoned.
options.misconception: generalises from a survey that records variation

options.text: Revived facades are younger on average than the others, so the practice is a modern fashion.
options.misconception: reads a date average as proof the practice began recently

options.text: Because the revived buildings are scattered in date, the survey shows the choice had no pattern.
options.misconception: calls a clustered pattern random because one column varies

questions.explanation: The clustering of revivals by decade shows the practice answering to a particular climate of taste. The never-abandoned, modern-fashion and no-pattern readings each flatten a real distribution.
questions.hint: Group the revivals by decade before reading the results.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how patronage shapes the picture a patron ends up commissioning
questions.stem: A transport engineer designing an underpass mural asks how patronage shapes which picture a client ends up commissioning.

answer.exemplar: Patronage shapes the commission by fixing who decides the subject, what message the image must carry, and what the viewer is expected to take from it, so the workshop's freedom is real but bounded by the terms the patron sets and the audience he has in view.

questions.explanation: The patron supplies the subject, the use and the audience, which together shape the picture. The idea that painters choose freely, or that patrons never intervene, both miss the negotiation.
questions.hint: Ask who set the subject and who the image was for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission and its stated purpose
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of a commission fee left for the master's own work
questions.stem: A contract for a chapel altarpiece pays 480 florins; materials cost 168 and assistants' wages 192 florins; what percentage of the fee is left for the master's own work?
questions.explanation: The remainder is 480 minus 168 minus 192, which is 120 florins, and 120 divided by 480 is 25 per cent. Taking materials alone would leave a much larger share.
questions.hint: Subtract both costs from the fee before taking a share.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the features that made a window legible to its viewers

stimulus.body: A glazier's note for a chapel window lists the panels from bottom to top: at the foot, the donor kneeling with a small offering; above, a row of seated figures reading; higher, a scene of a miracle; and at the head, a figure in light. A second glazier, hired two years later, states that he followed the first man's sequence exactly.

questions.stem: Given the glazier's note, what made this window legible to the congregation?

options.text: A deliberate order of scenes and figures, read upward, that let a viewer follow a single narrative.
The vividness of the colours, which made the window the most attractive object in the chapel.
options.misconception: credits only colour and ignores the ordered sequence

options.text: The donor's small offering, which paid for the window and therefore explains its layout.
options.misconception: treats a payment clue as the cause of the composition

options.text: The second glazier's statement, which proves the design was the first man's personal invention.
options.misconception: reads a continuity record as proof of individual invention

questions.explanation: Legibility came from the tiered order, which a viewer could read as a sequence. The colour, payment and invention readings each point to something present but miss the ordering.
questions.hint: Follow the note from the foot of the window to its head.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an inscription adds to a commemorative picture
questions.stem: Identify who the inscription names first and why; then choose the option that best explains what an inscription adds to a picture.

options.text: It fixes a named beneficiary and a stated purpose, so the picture can be read as a record of an arrangement.
It proves the picture was made by the artist whose signature is cut below the frame.
options.misconception: assumes an inscription always names the maker

options.text: It replaces the need for the picture, since the written word says everything the image should say.
options.misconception: treats inscription and image as rival carriers of meaning

options.text: It shows the monument was already old when the picture was added, which dates the picture by its carrier.
options.misconception: dates a picture from the age of the support beneath it

questions.explanation: An inscription anchors a picture in a named arrangement, so viewers know what it was for. The maker, rival and dating readings each pull the inscription away from that function.
questions.hint: Ask what an inscription tells that a face cannot.

questions.topic: A court image and its political claim
questions.learningObjective: Classify the kind of claim a court portrait in a great hall makes
questions.stem: A sound engineer is asked to reduce echoes in a hall whose walls carry a large state portrait; what kind of claim does that portrait make?

options.text: A political claim about rightful authority, made through the ranked figures and the setting around them.
A decorative claim, since any large painting in a hall is primarily a device for covering bare wall.
options.misconception: reduces a political image to a plain covering of surface

options.text: A commercial claim, since portraits of rulers were often made to advertise the workshop that painted them.
options.misconception: reads the image as advertising rather than as argument

options.text: A technical claim, since the picture demonstrates the painter's ability to handle a difficult wall surface.
options.misconception: reads the image as a display of painterly technique

questions.explanation: A court portrait argues about authority, and the room's acoustics are incidental to that argument. The decorative, commercial and technical readings each set the claim aside.
questions.hint: Consider what a viewer is meant to conclude in that room.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what a technical survey of a dated panel series establishes
questions.stem: A dated series of 30 panels is examined for pigment, ground preparation, punchwork and gilding; what can such a technical survey establish?

options.text: That the panels belong to a workshop working to shared methods in a particular period.
That the panels were painted by a single hand, because technique is never shared between makers.
options.misconception: assumes shared method rules out a single author

options.text: That the panels are all later copies, because a technical record never shows the date of a work.
options.misconception: holds that technical evidence can never indicate dating

options.text: That the panels were made for export, because imported works always use a different ground.
options.misconception: links a technical feature directly to a place of export

questions.explanation: Shared technical habits place panels together in time and workshop. The single-hand, never-dates and export readings each claim a certainty the evidence cannot supply either way.
questions.hint: Ask what shared methods can date, and what they cannot.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret how one patron varies subject and scale for different audiences

A second letter from the same merchant asks for a devotional panel for his private chapel.

questions.stem: Given these two requests, what does the change between them show?

options.text: The patron adapts the subject and scale to the audience and use he has in mind for each picture.
The patron's taste changes between the two letters, so the first request should be read as an accident.

questions.stem: A public library's designer asks how the patron's interest reaches the surface of a picture and its setting.

answer.exemplar: The patron's interest reaches the surface through the subject, the scale and position of figures, the inscriptions and the choice of building, so the same interest can be read at several levels at once, and a viewer who cannot read the text still meets the claim in the picture's arrangement and its setting.

questions.explanation: Patronage works through several channels at once, so the claim survives in the arrangement even when the text cannot be read. An account that reduces it to one inscription or one subject misses the pattern.
questions.hint: List the places in the scheme where the patron shows.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission and its stated purpose
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the master's share of a commission fee after all costs
questions.stem: A contract pays 480 florins for an altarpiece; materials cost 168 florins and assistants' wages 192 florins; what percentage of the fee is left for the master's own share?
questions.explanation: The master's share is 480 minus 168 minus 192, which is 120 florins, and 120 is a quarter of 480. Ignoring the assistants' wages would overstate the remaining share.
questions.hint: Take both cost lines off the fee before finding the share.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how a shutter and a calendar made a window serve a yearly cycle

stimulus.body: A congregation's book for a year lists the sequence of feasts on which the window was read, and marks beside each feast the section of the window that was shown that day. The book also records that the window had a sliding shutter allowing the lower register to be covered. On several feast days the entry notes only the upper register was shown.

questions.stem: Given the congregation book, what does the record show about the window?

options.text: That its registers were usable separately, so the window could serve the yearly cycle of readings.
That the window was rebuilt each year, since its subject changed with the feasts of the year.
options.misconception: turns a sequence of readings into a yearly rebuilding

options.text: That the lower register was damaged, which is why the shutter was there to hide the broken glass.
options.misconception: infers damage where the book records a choice

options.text: That the congregation was small, since so few members could follow the full reading of the window.
options.misconception: infers attendance from a note about which registers were shown

questions.explanation: A shutter that could cover a register, combined with a calendar of readings, shows a window designed to serve a cycle. The rebuilt, damaged-glass and small-congregation readings each misread the record.
questions.hint: Read the shutter entry together with the calendar.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a donor's inscription commits a memorial to
questions.stem: Work out what a donor's inscription commits the memorial to, and then choose the option that follows from it.

options.text: It binds the monument to an arrangement between donor, church and the living, which the picture records.
It fixes the price the monument cost, so the picture is mainly evidence of the donor's wealth.
options.misconception: reads a commemorative text as a financial record

options.text: It dates the artist's apprenticeship, since memorials often list where a painter was trained.
options.misconception: supplies a training detail the inscription does not carry

options.text: It ends the donor's involvement, since the words were carved once and the contract was then closed.
options.misconception: treats a carved text as the end of an arrangement

questions.explanation: An inscription states terms of commemoration, so the picture illustrates an ongoing arrangement between donor, church and viewers. The price, apprenticeship and closed-contract readings substitute a different subject.
questions.hint: Ask what the carved words commit the parties to.
